'Missing lead' in Flint water pipes confirms cause of crisis

They switched water sources, the new source had a different hardness level and suddenly lead piping was able to dissolve into the water.

It's simple ion exchange. In fact, Flint is far from the only town with this problem. Any area with typically hard water will probably have significant amounts of legacy lead piping that's still in use. The lead can't dissolve into the water because calcium and magnesium edge it out - but start running something else through that pipe and you'll get your lead right quick.
Lead piping? Is lead still used in the water system in the US? Doesn't sound right to me.

Lead is a soft metal that naturally resists corrosion, so it's actually an excellent metal for underground piping.

Once people realized lead was bad for you they started swapping things out, but it's incredibly expensive to replace underground pipes. Most municipalities had a "phase it out as we do routine repairs" policy that worked well enough. But the lazier or poorer areas might have just "forgotten" to get around to it...

Enter Flint. They had quite a bit of lead piping, but it was harmless because the water going through the pipes were saturated with other hard ions. Lead will dissolve into water, but calcium and magnesium want it more. So lead gets out-competed for the space and stays a metal pipe in hard water. The officials probably had a "no harm no foul" attitude to the whole thing, which was largely true.

When Flint changed their water source, the new water didn't have those hard ions and so the lead had nothing forcing it to stay in solid form. It happily began dissolving into the water and things became the shitstorm we all know and love today. Officials trying to cover their ass and budgets unable to solve the problem, etc. etc.
